title: Negative Expansion Materials Resist Warpage
gist: Thermally induced warpage from coefficient-of-thermal-expansion mismatch is one of the biggest constraints on growing package substrates, interposers and panels, and existing levers like silicon thinning conflict with high-power thermal needs. A newly commercial class of negative thermal expansion fillers from Mitsubishi Chemical Group — inorganic, lattice-caged materials mixed into epoxy molding compounds and underfills — offers a way to tune effective CTE downward, but adoption hinges on temperature range, mixing uniformity, and alpha-particle-emitting impurities.

themes.theme: Warpage as the gating constraint on larger packages and panels

insights.claim: Thermally induced warpage is one of the biggest issues holding back the constant enlargement of package substrates, interposers and panels, because the larger the bonded area, the greater the likelihood that edge connections are poor or fail altogether.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Identifies the physical ceiling on the package-size scaling that AI accelerator roadmaps depend on — a materials problem, not a lithography one.
insights.quote: It’s one of the biggest issues holding back the constant enlargement of package substrates, interposers, and panels.
insights.locator: Warpage as the enemy

insights.claim: Excess warpage defeats standard manufacturing equipment features before bonding even happens: vacuum chucks pull warpage down, but if warpage is too high the tool cannot get a good vacuum.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Warpage limits are enforced by installed equipment, meaning the problem shows up as yield and handling loss across existing OSAT tool fleets, not just at final test.
insights.quote: The vacuum chucks will pull the warpage down, but if the warpage is too high, then you won’t get a good vacuum
insights.locator: Warpage as the enemy — Olmstead quote

insights.claim: It is theoretically impossible to eliminate all warpage where a CTE difference exists, so the engineering question is not prevention but how much warpage is too much and what levers can control it.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Reframes warpage as a tolerance-budgeting discipline, which is why modeling and materials tuning — not a single fix — become recurring spend.
insights.quote: It’s theoretically impossible to stop all warpage if there is a CTE difference.
insights.locator: Warpage as the enemy

insights.claim: Thinning silicon reduces warping by reducing the impact of low-CTE silicon, but in the extreme the silicon merely follows the shape of whatever it is attached to, and nobody wants really thin silicon for managing high power.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: The conventional warpage lever directly conflicts with high-power AI package thermal requirements, which is why new materials rather than thinner die are being pursued.
insights.quote: In the extreme, you can make it super thin, and then it can follow the shape of whatever I’m attached to. But that ends up being a problem, because nobody wants really thin silicon for managing high power.
insights.locator: Warpage as the enemy — Kelly quote

insights.claim: Glass panels could raise warpage by three orders of magnitude relative to today's practice — from micrometers of warpage to potentially millimeters — as panel size grows.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: A concrete magnitude estimate for why glass-core substrate adoption may be slower and more materials-dependent than roadmaps assume.
insights.quote: Today we talk about micrometers of warpage, but with glass, it could be even larger — millimeters, maybe.
insights.locator: Warpage as the enemy — Lin quote

insights.claim: Epoxy molding compound used for fillers and underfill is the leverage point for warpage control because it fills all the major gaps inside the package and therefore affects everything it touches when temperature changes.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Explains why molding compound and underfill suppliers — not substrate makers alone — capture the value from solving large-package warpage.
insights.quote: It fills all the major gaps inside the package, so when the temperature changes, it can affect everything it touches.
insights.locator: Going against the grain

themes.theme: Negative thermal expansion mechanism: lattices and caged flow

insights.claim: Rather than relying solely on the few substances that genuinely shrink when heated, companies are focusing on mixtures of materials with a lattice structure that resists the urge to expand, using them as underfill and molding compound to add rigidity for larger packages while keeping warpage in check.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: The commercial path is composite formulation, not discovery of exotic pure NTE compounds — which makes it a formulation-chemistry business.
insights.quote: Rather than relying solely on the few substances that can shrink, companies are focusing on mixtures of materials with a lattice structure that can resist the urge to expand.
insights.locator: Lede

insights.claim: The performance of a negative-expansion additive is governed by the structure of the filler network — house-of-cards, rigid-rod, or tetrahedral lattices each behave differently — rather than by the chemical identity of the material alone.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Competitive moat sits in network architecture and functionalization know-how, which is harder to copy than a compound formula.
insights.quote: It’s more of a network thing than a material thing
insights.locator: Going against the grain — Bhatt quote

insights.claim: The difference between filler types is analogous to logs in a river versus clay in water: carbon fiber forms a reinforcing rigid-rod network that only partially restricts flow, while a dispersed particulate like clay changes viscosity and literally restricts movement.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: A usable mental model for judging which filler chemistries can actually suppress expansion versus merely reinforce a resin.
insights.quote: If I use the logs in water, it is going to have little impact on the ability of water to flow.
insights.locator: Going against the grain — Bhatt quote

insights.claim: Shrinkage and expansion are treated rheologically as low shear-rate flows, so caging a material in a matrix changes the dynamics of that flow and can even produce slight contraction on heating by reorienting molecules in the structure.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Recasting thermal expansion as a flow problem opens design space beyond searching for naturally NTE compounds.
insights.quote: A lot of people will talk about shrinkage and expansion, but to me, those are low shear-rate flows rheologically
insights.locator: Caught in a cage — Bhatt quote

insights.claim: Self-assembly is where chemistry enters: the filler components must be functionalized appropriately so they arrange themselves into a house-of-cards lattice whose resultant matrix has a negative CTE.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Surface functionalization capability, not raw material supply, determines who can actually produce working NTE fillers at scale.
insights.quote: Self-assembly is where chemistry comes into the picture — you have to make sure that these things are functionalized appropriately so they arrange themselves in a certain way.
insights.locator: Caught in a cage — Bhatt quote

insights.claim: The restraining matrix can burst under the pressure of the expanding material it cages, and that failure mode is simply melting — the point at which the entire configuration falls apart — bounded by the matrix's own thermal capability.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Defines the upper operating limit of caged NTE composites, which matters for high-temperature assembly steps and reliability qualification.
insights.quote: If you have a matrix and you melt it and it starts flowing, that’s the bursting analogy
insights.locator: Caught in a cage — Bhatt quote

insights.claim: Reinforcement changes the flow characteristics of the encased material but does very little for its thermal transitional behavior and will never change the glass transition or melt transition temperature.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Sets a hard boundary on what NTE fillers can fix — they buy CTE tuning, not extended thermal operating windows.
insights.quote: It will never change the glass transition or the melt transition temperature.
insights.locator: Caught in a cage — Bhatt quote

insights.claim: The goal is not a zero-CTE material but tuning a compound's effective CTE to minimize the mismatch among die, substrate and encapsulant, thereby reducing stress and package warpage.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Reframes the product as a tunable CTE knob per package stack, implying customized formulations per customer rather than a single commodity grade.
insights.quote: Our negative-CTE filler contracts as temperature rises, offsetting the natural expansion of the resin
insights.locator: Caught in a cage — Bhatt quote

insights.claim: Negative-CTE fillers can be added to a polymer, which typically has a very high CTE compared to inorganics, to pull the polymer matrix's overall CTE closer to that of the metal layers and other device components.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Names the specific mismatch — organic layers versus metal and inorganic layers — that NTE fillers target inside advanced packages.
insights.quote: Reducing or modulating the CTE of organic layers to be closer to the inorganic layers helps in reducing warpage and overall stress build-up in a device.
insights.locator: Warpage as the enemy — Prenger quote

themes.theme: Scarcity of true NTE materials and the inorganic-only constraint

insights.claim: The number of negative-CTE materials is very limited, with β-eucryptite actively used as ceramics for chucks and parts in certain tooling and zirconium tungstate used as an additive for various mold compounds and underfills.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Names the only two incumbent NTE materials in practical use — a very narrow supply base that constrains how fast the approach can scale.
insights.quote: β-eucryptite is actively used as ceramics for chunks and parts in certain tooling, and zirconium tungstate is being utilized as an additive for various types of mold compounds and underfills.
insights.locator: NTE materials debut — Prenger quote

insights.claim: Zirconium tungstate does not occur in nature and is one of the human-made substances exhibiting negative thermal expansion in all three dimensions, and such materials are very challenging to design.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Three-dimensional NTE is rare and synthetic, so the supply chain for these fillers is manufactured chemistry rather than mined material.
insights.quote: With NTE in all three dimensions, it’s one of the human-made NTE substances.
insights.locator: NTE materials debut

insights.claim: Designing new negative-CTE materials exists only in the realm of inorganic materials, because for almost every polymer noted to have negative CTE the effect is negative in only one dimension — which limits organic materials exclusively to adding inorganic fillers.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Structurally rules out an all-organic solution, locking the value into inorganic filler suppliers who feed the polymer formulators.
insights.quote: for almost every polymer material that is noted to have negative CTE, it is negative only in one dimension, not in three dimensions
insights.locator: NTE materials debut — Prenger quote

insights.claim: True NTE behavior often occurs only within specific temperature ranges and may be associated with a phase change, as with water, which expands between 3.98°C and 0°C as more of it takes on the less dense ice configuration.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Explains why temperature-range coverage is the key qualification hurdle for these materials rather than peak performance at one temperature.
insights.quote: A variety of materials can exhibit true negative thermal expansion (NTE) behavior, although it often occurs within specific temperature ranges.
insights.locator: Going against the grain

themes.theme: Commercialization: Mitsubishi's debut and the adoption gates

insights.claim: Although NTE materials have been a research topic for a while, they have recently become commercially available from Mitsubishi Chemical Group as an inorganic material that can be mixed with organic epoxy resins to customize the epoxy's CTE, and is also offered pre-mixed with resin.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Marks the transition of NTE from lab curiosity to a purchasable packaging material, with Mitsubishi holding first-mover position.
insights.quote: they’ve recently become available from Mitsubishi Chemical Group
insights.locator: NTE materials debut

insights.claim: If this proves out and other materials companies follow suit, negative-expansion filler could become a standard formulation for semiconductor packaging.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Flags a potential new standard line item in the packaging materials bill of materials, with follow-on entrants likely if qualification succeeds.
insights.quote: If this proves out and other materials companies follow suit, this could become a standard formulation for semiconductor packaging.
insights.locator: NTE materials debut

insights.claim: Commercial success for NTE packaging materials requires performing over a wide temperature range covering both processing and higher-temperature manufacturing operations, mixing easily and uniformly into resins, and not introducing unexpected effects from alpha-particle emissions caused by impurities.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: A three-item qualification checklist that will decide adoption — alpha emission in particular ties material purity directly to soft-error reliability.
insights.quote: They must also not introduce unexpected effects from alpha-particle emissions caused by impurities.
insights.locator: NTE materials debut

insights.claim: Warpage is modeled beforehand and then controlled through a set of levers, making pre-assembly simulation a standard part of OSAT warpage management.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Simulation tooling is already embedded in packaging workflows, creating pull-through for EDA and multiphysics vendors alongside new materials.
insights.quote: We do a certain level of modeling to model the warpage beforehand, and then there’s certain levers you can pull to control the warpage
insights.locator: Warpage as the enemy — Olmstead quote

insights.claim: If NTE materials work as planned, they represent another step toward enabling larger packages and panels — tying a materials-chemistry advance directly to the package-size scaling that advanced packaging roadmaps require.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Positions specialty filler chemistry as an enabler of the large-format packaging that AI compute economics depend on.
insights.quote: If all works as planned, this may be yet another step toward enabling larger packages and panels.
insights.locator: NTE materials debut, closing
